SECTION 4 CAPACITY REVIEW
General A review of the hydraulic and treatment capacities of the Winchester WTP was performed to determine the current capacity and possible future capacity given the limitations of each process and the interconnected system as a whole. The hydraulic capacity is related to the piping, pumping, volume and flow control systems, which limit the ability of the water to flow through individual unit operations and through the interconnected system as a whole. The treatment capacity is related to the ability of each treatment unit process to meet regulatory requirements or generally accepted industry standards, whichever is applicable.
The Winchester WTP has a current rated plant capacity of 12 mgd. This is a treatment capacity limitation determined by the four existing filters. Most of the existing equipment and treatment processes already have capacities exceeding that value. The plant was designed to be expanded to a nominal capacity of 18 mgd. This is also a treatment capacity limitation based on an ultimate build out of six filters using the same media as the existing four filters. Hydraulic and treatment capacities are discussed and evaluated separately.
The City currently has water rights on the North Umpqua River totaling 20 mgd and is investigating the possibility of obtaining additional rights from that source. This topic is discussed in greater detail in the Long-Range Water Supply Plan for the City of Roseburg. Since the existing water rights exceed 18 mgd, and because there is the possibility of obtaining additional rights, this section also analyzes the ability of individual unit operations to accept higher flow rates, between 18 and 24 mgd. For each unit operation, the likely ultimate hydraulic and treatment capacity is analyzed, modifications required to achieve the higher rate are identified, and suggested improvements are noted if they appear to be feasible. Figure 4-1 at the end of this section shows the general site plan for the existing Winchester WTP.
Hydraulic Capacity Evaluation
General
The maximum raw water pumping rate with all raw water pumps operating is nominally 22 mgd; however, during a test on June 24, 2003, the total combined flow of all four raw water pumps was 20.9 mgd. The maximum instantaneous flow rate of finished water from the high service pump station is nominally 16 mgd with all finished water pumps operating; however, the maximum actually achieved is about 14 mgd.

The plant currently operates continuously throughout each day on a “24/7” basis to keep the terminal reservoirs on Reservoir Hill full to meet demands in the City’s distribution system. The plant flow rate is typically adjusted on a daily basis, and occasionally more frequently when required, as water demands fluctuate. As discussed in Section 2, the plant flow rate has ranged from approximately 3.5 mgd during low demand periods to 11.6 mgd during a recent peak summer day.
Existing Hydraulic Profile
Figure 4-2 at the end of this section presents the hydraulic profile of the plant. The hydraulic profile was developed during the original design of the Winchester WTP for a maximum instantaneous flow of 18 mgd. Figure 4-1 has been updated, based on field tests conducted for this analysis, for a maximum flow of 22 mgd. The key hydraulic control features of the plant include:
River water levels and intake pumping capacity Hydraulic capacity of the 30-inch raw water pipeline to the flocculation/sedimentation basin Hydraulic capacity of the overflow weir at the outlet of the flocculation/sedimentation basin Hydraulic capacity of the 42-inch settled water pipeline delivering water to the filters Filter and pipe gallery hydraulics, including minimum water level inside the filters, for optimum performance and adequate available headloss for filter operations Filter underdrain and piping system capacity to the clearwell Hydraulic capacity of the overflow weir in the clearwell High service pumping capacity from the clearwell into the transmission system Finished water transmission pipeline capacity Backwash piping and pumping capacity Wastewater pump station and force main capacity Washwater and solids handling system capacity
Hydraulic capacity issues associated with each of these features are described in detail below.
Intake and Raw Water Pumping Capacity
The existing intake is equipped with 4 vertical turbine pumps, one with a capacity of 2,800 gpm (4.0 mgd) at 49 feet of total dynamic head (TDH) and three, each with a capacity of 4,200 gpm (6.0 mgd) at 49 feet of TDH. The smaller pump, Pump No. 1, has a 50 hp motor and the larger pumps, Pump Nos. 2, 3, and 4, have 75 hp motors.
All of the spaces provided for pumps are filled at the Winchester WTP intake. According to current planning and operating conventions within the water industry, firm pumping capacity is defined as the maximum flow achievable with one of the largest installed pumps out of service; therefore, the nominal firm capacity of the intake is approximately 16 mgd. Raw Water Pipeline Capacity to the Flocculation/Sedimentation Basin
The raw water pumps discharge into an underground 30-inch diameter steel raw water pipeline which delivers raw water to the flocculation/sedimentation basin, entering on the northeast corner of the structure. The steel pipe has a ¼-inch wall thickness. A 30-inch magnetic flow meter was installed on this pipeline in a below-grade vault in 2002, replacing a meter previously located at the inlet of the raw water pipeline into the rapid mix basin. The velocity, velocity head and head loss for the existing raw water pipeline at various flows are presented in Table 4-1.

As shown in the table, velocities through the 30-inch raw water pipeline exceed 6.0 fps at flows slightly over 18 mgd. The maximum desirable velocity in a transmission main of this type is typically 6.0 fps. even at the higher velocities that will exist above 18 mgd. The headloss associated with higher flow through the existing pipeline will ultimately raise the system total dynamic head (TDH), thus reducing the capacity of the raw water pump station. To account for this, replacing pumps with a higher pumping head may be necessary to compensate for this increased headloss. If the plant is expanded beyond 18 mgd, there will be an opportunity to adjust the design head as necessary at that time.
Rapid Mix and Flocculation/Sedimentation Basin
Raw water flows first into a rapid mix basin and then into the flocculation/sedimentation basin. There are two rapid mix basins in parallel, but currently only one rapid mixer is operated at any given time. The basin design provides for the addition of a second, parallel flocculation and sedimentation basin to increase the plant capacity to a nominal 18 mgd. Under those conditions, both rapid mix basins will be operated in parallel at the higher flows.

Section 2 discussed the design features of the plant’s pretreatment system including rapid mix, flocculation and sedimentation. The single existing basin is rated at 12 mgd and was designed to be expanded with a parallel basin for an ultimate nominal treatment capacity of 18 mgd, but with approximately 24 mgd of hydraulic capacity. As previously discussed, this basin has been able to provide excellent pretreatment prior to filtration at sustained flows up to 11.5 mgd during the warm weather, low turbidity raw water conditions. Normal plant flows during high turbidity, colder water conditions have ranged from 3.5 to 5.0 mgd.
Settled solids from the basin are continuously removed by a chain-and-flight system. Settled water flows from the basin via the launders into a settled water channel located at the south end of the basin. The settled water then flows to the filters via a 42-inch pipeline.
The maximum water elevation in the basin is in the raw water influent channel. At 12 mgd, There is a triangular launder weir in the sedimentation basin with invert elevation of approximately 465.83 feet. The bottoms of the 12-inch deep launder troughs in the sedimentation basin are approximately elevation 464.63 feet. The freeboard from the top of maximum water surface to the top of walls is approximately 1.5 feet which is adequate.
The basin has an overflow weir to accommodate unplanned filter influent valve shutdowns or raw water flows into the basin that exceed the filter capacity. The overflow weir is located in the settled water collection channel at the south end of the basin above a disposal channel drained by a pipeline. The overflow weir elevation is at 465.0 feet, approximately 1.0 feet higher than the normal filter operating level. The weir is approximately 9 feet long with a capacity of approximately 12 mgd, assuming a 9-inch water depth over the weir. The drain pipe is 30-inches in diameter, has a capacity of approximately 10 mgd, and delivers this flow to a diversion manhole with a weir. Under normal conditions sedimentation basin overflows are directed to the wastewater pump station, but if the pump station cannot handle the flow the water flows over the weir inside the diversion manhole and then to the river. A second overflow weir will be constructed along with the second flocculation/sedimentation basin when the plant is expanded; thus, the overflow system is adequate for an ultimate maximum plant capacity of 24 mgd.
The settled water pipeline to the filters is a 42-inch diameter steel pipe. At 18 mgd the pipeline velocity will be 2.9 fps and at 24 mgd the pipeline velocity would be 3.9 fps. Although these velocities are not excessive, this pipe could be the largest contributor to headloss at high flows. During a flow test conducted on September 14, 2006, the head loss through the pipe was measured at 2.8-inches at a flow rate of 13.1 mgd. Under these conditions, the water surface in the settled water channel was approximately 6-inches below the basin overflow weir. Depending upon where the new settled water pipe connects to the existing settled water pipe, the head loss at 24 mgd would be several inches greater.

Through such careful design, it may be possible to avoid raising the overflow weir on the existing basin. The ultimate hydraulic capacity of the two basins in parallel is limited primarily by the settled water pipeline and that ultimate capacity is 22 to 24 mgd.
Filters, Filter Effluent and Filter-to-Waste Piping
Section 2 provides basic information on the design and performance of the filters. Settled water flows through the filter influent channel and enters each filter via a 20-inch pipe with isolation valve. The normal filter operating level ranges from 463 to 464 feet as controlled by the filter effluent flow control system. This water level provides 5 to 6 feet of submergence over the top of the filter media. A filter effluent modulating valve is used to maintain this water level in each filter. As headloss increases, the valve opens further. Each filter consists of two bays. The water flows down through the media, the support gravel and the underdrain of each filter bay. The water then flows into the filter piping gallery through 16-inch pipes that individually drain each filter bay and is combined into an 18-inch filter effluent pipe that is common to the two bays within a filter. The filtered water flows through the 18-inch effluent pipe, a propeller flow meter, the filter effluent modulating butterfly valve and then into the unbaffled clearwell area underneath the filters. Each filter empties directly into the clearwell through its own 18-inch effluent pipe, thus each filter’s effluent enters the clearwell at a different location.
The normal maximum water level in the treated water storage area and clearwell is 449.0 feet, six-inches below the elevation of an overflow weir located beneath the high service pump station. The clearwell is normally operated between about 446.5 feet and 448 feet, which provides a total filter driving head of approximately 15 to 17.5 feet from filter water level to treated water storage level. The alarm signifying terminal filter headloss is currently set at 11.0 feet. Plans were made with the original design to add two more filters to expand capacity.
As discussed below, the current 3 mgd filter rating is a treatment capacity limitation rather than a hydraulic limitation. Hydraulically, the piping into and out of each basin can handle 4 mgd when the filter is filtering to the clearwell. With six filters, the total hydraulic capacity of the filters will be 24 mgd. Individual filter effluent flows into the clearwell are measured; however the requirements for straight-pipe both upstream and downstream of each filter effluent flow meter are not met, possibly reducing the accuracy of the meters. During a plant tour on September 14, 2006 the sum of the individual filter effluent meters was approximately 7 percent less than the flow determined by the more accurate magnetic flow meter measuring raw water flow.
The filter effluent piping arrangement currently prohibits the metering and modulating of filter-to-waste flows. Filter-to-waste flows can be estimated by calculating the difference between the raw water flow and the sum of the individual filter effluent flows. Based on this, it appears that the existing 8-inch filter-to-waste piping is too small to convey 3 mgd when filtering to waste. On a site visit to the plant on June 29, 2006, with filter No. 3 offline for
09-1015.401                                 Page 4-6                  WTP Preliminary Design Report
July 2009                                Capacity Review                           City of Roseburg

[p.113]
cleaning and a raw water flow of 9.1 mgd, the flow through filter No. 1 in filter-to-waste was estimated by calculating the difference between the raw water flow and the combined filter effluent flows through filters No. 2 and No. 4. The filter-to-waste flow was approximately 2 mgd while the flow through the other two filters was greater than 3.4 mgd.
It is desirable to modulate filter-to-waste flow to maintain relatively constant flow through all filters at all times. Rapid increases in flow through the media induce shear forces on the retained floc which can cause premature breakthrough. Inducing rapid flow changes in a conventional filter when the filter is operating near its treatment capacity is particularly problematic. When filter-to-waste piping is unable to pass the design filter flow, then the flow through all other filters on line increases while one filter is in filter-to-waste. This problem is more pronounced with fewer filters, when the filters are operating near their design flow and when the difference between the filter design flow and the filter-to-waste flow is high.
In addition to the hydraulic capacity limitations of the filter-to-waste piping, the current location of the filter effluent sample point prohibits measurement of turbidity during filter-to- waste. For all the above stated reasons, changes in the filter effluent and filter-to-waste piping are desirable.
Options for this work vary depending upon the extent to which the City desires to monitor and control filter-to-waste. It may be possible to achieve more accurate effluent flow measurement by simply installing a different meter while using the existing piping configuration. In addition, relocating the sample point would enable measurement of filter- to-waste turbidity; thus, the lowest cost option would be to change the type of effluent meter and the location of the sample point without reconfiguring the filter effluent piping. This option would not provide for measurement and control of filter-to-waste flow and it would not provide for the increased piping size needed to pass more than 2 mgd during filter-to- waste. To provide measurement and control of filter-to-waste flow, and to allow for filter-to- waste at the same rate as filtering to the clearwell, Although this is the more expensive alternative, it is the one that brings the greatest benefit.
Given that the existing filter-to-waste piping does not appear to convey more than 2 mgd, any plan to increase the WTP capacity beyond 18 mgd may require reconfiguring the piping since the difference between the existing filter-to-waste flow and the higher filter design flow would be even more pronounced.
Clearwell
The clearwell and treated water storage at the Winchester WTP are comprised of three interconnected areas described as follows:
09-1015.401                                  Page 4-7                   WTP Preliminary Design Report
July 2009                                 Capacity Review                            City of Roseburg
[1 recommendation clause(s) withheld]

[p.114]
1. Unbaffled area under the four filters with a maximum storage volume of approximately 170,000 gallons at 10.5 foot water depth.
2. Baffled clearwell area underneath the chemical rooms and the blower room with a maximum storage volume of approximately 324,000 gallons at 10.5 foot water depth.
3. Unbaffled area underneath the high service pump room with a maximum storage volume of approximately 133,000 gallon at 10.5 foot water depth.
The total maximum treated water storage volume of 627,000 gallons represents approximately 75 minutes (1.26 hours) of storage at the current maximum plant flow of 12 mgd. This assumes that all the treated water in the clearwell is available as storage; however, in addition to providing finished water storage, the clearwell serves as the wetwell for the high service and backwash pumps and provides disinfection contact time. During a backwash, the level in the clearwell drops about 1.0 feet. To ensure disinfection contact time, thus the actual treated water volume available as storage is less than the total clearwell volume. Disinfection contact time is a treatment unit operation, so it is discussed elsewhere in this section under Treatment Process Capacity Evaluation. In addition, a discussion of the clearwell’s current ability to meet disinfection (CT) requirements at various flows is presented in Section 3.
There are two clearwell overflows, one located in the high service pump station and the other located below Filter No. 3. The high service pump station clearwell overflow weir is at elevation 449.5 feet with a weir length of approximately 9 feet. The overflow is located in the northwest corner of the high service pump station. At 1 foot of water depth over the weir, the overflow capacity is approximately 19 mgd. The overflow water is discharged into an overflow chamber with inside dimensions of 4.5 feet by 4.5 feet. The water then flows into an 18-inch diameter pipeline which directs emergency overflows to an outfall on the bank of the North Umpqua River. The overflow weir and piping is sufficient to handle clearwell overflows up to 19 mgd.
The clearwell overflow located below Filter No. 3 is at an elevation of 450.00 feet with a weir length of approximately 15 feet. This overflow discharges to the backwash waste channel which flows to the wastewater pump station and to the river if the station cannot handle the flow. The high service pump station clearwell will overflow first until the water level exceeds 450.00 feet, then water will overflow both weirs. Combined, the two overflow weirs can accommodate an ultimate plant flow of 24 mgd.
During current normal operating conditions, the high service pumps operate to maintain the clearwell level relatively constant between approximately 8 feet and 10 feet depth, which is 3 to 1 feet below the overflow weir. The level drops by about 1-feet when a filter is backwashed. One filter backwash uses 65,000 to 75,000 gallons of water with the higher backwash volume used during the summer. Since all four filters are backwashed once per day, approximately 260,000 to 300,000 gallons of finished water is used daily for
09-1015.401                                Page 4-8                 WTP Preliminary Design Report
July 2009                               Capacity Review                          City of Roseburg
[1 recommendation clause(s) withheld]

[p.115]
backwashing. The clearwell level control is accomplished by manually throttling valves on the discharge piping of a raw water pump and a finished water pump to achieve somewhat stable operating conditions.
As discussed above in this section under the river intake and high service pump station paragraphs, the City is in the process of installing new variable-frequency drives (VFDs) on one raw water pump and one finished water pump to more accurately balance the flows to maintain a constant clearwell level while avoiding the need for valve throttling. These drives will also improve energy efficiency. The finished water pumping rate can then be decreased during backwashes to maintain the clearwell level as close to full as possible at all times.
It is generally considered desirable that a WTP maintain a minimum clearwell volume of approximately 60 minutes of detention time at the plant’s peak flow rate. This criterion is currently being met at the 12 mgd plant capacity, although only if one assumes the entire clearwell volume is available as storage. When the plant is expanded with two additional filters, an additional 85,000 gallons of treated water storage will be added under Filters 5 and 6, At the expanded plant capacity of 18 mgd, the maximum detention time would then be 57 minutes, which approximates the minimum desirable time. At plant capacities greater than 18 mgd, the treated water storage at the plant would be considered less than optimal. At 24 mgd using the 1-hour criteria, the suggested minimum clearwell volume is 1,000,000 gallons which is 288,000 gallons more than will be available when the ultimate buildout of six filters has been achieved. There is extremely limited space on the existing site to construct additional treated water storage. A detailed discussion regarding clearwell improvements for future expansion that may provide the ability to meet disinfection requirements is presented in the treatment capacity evaluation portion of this section.
High Service Pump Station
The station is equipped with 4 vertical turbine, high service pumps including:
One pump (No. 1) rated at 1,400 gpm (2.0 mgd) at 305 feet TDH, with a 150 hp motor Three pumps (Nos. 2, 3 and 4) each rated at 2,800 gpm (4.0 mgd) at 305 feet TDH, with 300 hp motors.
All four of these constant speed pumps were installed in the Phase 2, High Service Pump Station phase, of the WTP project in 1987-1988. There is space provided in the pump station and on the discharge header for two additional pumps. The City recently installed a VFD on Pump No. 2. Finished Water Transmission Pipelines – WTP to Reservoir Hill
The 30-inch finished water transmission main from the plant connects to two transmission mains on the plant site. These mains are a 20-inch outside diameter steel main with a 3/16- inch thick wall and a 30-inch diameter Class 50 ductile iron main. These mains constitute the northerly portion of the City’s transmission system to terminal reservoirs on Reservoir Hill. This system was the subject of a study entitled “Preliminary Engineering Study for Water Transmission System for City of Roseburg, Oregon, July, 1986”. This study evaluated the hydraulics of the existing system, evaluated the condition of the existing pipelines, analyzed alternative sizes and routes for pipelines for improved transmission system capacity,

The study provided key hydraulic information needed for the design of the treatment plant’s finished water pumping system (pumps and piping) and the surge control facilities.
Phase 1 consisted of construction of approximately 9,400 feet of new parallel transmission piping and demolition of an existing booster pumping station. Phase 2 consisted of the easterly and southerly extension of a new 27-inch diameter transmission main approximately 1,600 feet long from the above intersection to the reservoir complex on Reservoir Hill. This main would parallel an existing 24-inch main. Based upon recent studies by the City and consultations with the project developer, it is anticipated that a new 30-inch main will be constructed initially as part of the development to replace the existing 27-inch main. A second parallel 30-inch main would be constructed in the future, thus completing the two-pipe transmission system between the plant and the terminal reservoirs.

Air Scour System The WTP has an air scour system for filter backwash. The system is supplied with low pressure air from a multi-stage centrifugal blower. The blower has a capacity of 1,050 scfm at 6.4 psi and is driven by a 60 hp motor. Low pressure air is directed to each of the filters through an 8-inch diameter air supply system. Air flow is controlled by an electrically operated butterfly valve. Air flow control using a control valve on a relief vent may provide for more precise air flow control.
Backwash Pumping and Piping The WTP is currently equipped with two constant-speed vertical turbine backwash pumps, each with a 50 hp motor, rated at 3,250 gpm at 41 feet TDH. Only one pump is required for
09-1015.401                                Page 4-12                WTP Preliminary Design Report
July 2009                               Capacity Review                          City of Roseburg
[7 recommendation clause(s) withheld]

[p.119]
backwashing each of the filter bays. The second pump serves as a spare/backup for emergencies. The backwash pumps discharge into a 16-inch diameter header that feeds backwash water to the individual filters. These pumps and the associated piping and valving are adequately sized for the existing filter configuration and filter type.
If the filter media is changed in the future to deep bed filters to achieve production rates higher than 18 mgd, higher backwash rates than these pumps can achieve may be required. It is estimated that the optimum backwash rate for these filter bays outfitted with deep bed media (up to 1.1 mm effective size anthracite) would be approximately 4,400 gpm. When the pumps were tested on September 14, 2006 with the modulating butterfly valve at approximately 45º open, the pumps produced 4,060 gpm, so the existing pumps may be able to achieve acceptable backwash rates with deep bed media. It is also possible that the existing pumps may be nearing their expected lifetime by the time the need for deep bed media occurs and could therefore be replaced.
Filter backwash water from each filter discharges through a 16-inch backwash drain pipeline into the backwash conveyance channel under the filter gallery floor slab. From the channel, flow is conveyed via a 24-inch diameter pipeline to a drain manhole and then through a 30- inch pipeline to the wastewater pump station. The new, larger pipeline will be capable of conveying a higher backwash flow in the future if a higher rate is needed to backwash a larger filter media. Wastewater Pump Station
The plant’s wastewater pump station collects filter backwash and other plant drainage discharges and pumps them to the plant’s solids handling system. The pump station consists of a wetwell containing three 35 hp submersible solids handling pumps, each with a capacity of approximately 1,500 gpm at 40 feet of TDH. Each pump has a 10-inch diameter discharge with 10-inch isolation and check valves. A 16-inch diameter transfer main carries the wastewater to backwash basins 1 and 2. The approximate firm capacity of this station is 3,000 gpm with one of the pumps out of service.
Solids and Washwater Handling Two new washwater and solids equalization/settling basins, plus the two new solids drying beds, were recently constructed by the City to replace the old lagoon and drying bed. Each basin has a maximum volume of approximately 300,000 gallons. Filter backwash, settled sludge and other plant drainage pumped from the wastewater pump station can be directed to either basin. SECTION 4 CAPACITY REVIEW
General A review of the hydraulic and treatment capacities of the Winchester WTP was performed to determine the current capacity and possible future capacity given the limitations of each process and the interconnected system as a whole. The hydraulic capacity is related to the piping, pumping, volume and flow control systems, which limit the ability of the water to flow through individual unit operations and through the interconnected system as a whole. The treatment capacity is related to the ability of each treatment unit process to meet regulatory requirements or generally accepted industry standards, whichever is applicable.
The Winchester WTP has a current rated plant capacity of 12 mgd. This is a treatment capacity limitation determined by the four existing filters. Most of the existing equipment and treatment processes already have capacities exceeding that value. The plant was designed to be expanded to a nominal capacity of 18 mgd. This is also a treatment capacity limitation based on an ultimate build out of six filters using the same media as the existing four filters. Hydraulic and treatment capacities are discussed and evaluated separately.
The City currently has water rights on the North Umpqua River totaling 20 mgd and is investigating the possibility of obtaining additional rights from that source. This topic is discussed in greater detail in the Long-Range Water Supply Plan for the City of Roseburg. Since the existing water rights exceed 18 mgd, and because there is the possibility of obtaining additional rights, this section also analyzes the ability of individual unit operations to accept higher flow rates, between 18 and 24 mgd. For each unit operation, the likely ultimate hydraulic and treatment capacity is analyzed, modifications required to achieve the higher rate are identified, and suggested improvements are noted if they appear to be feasible. Figure 4-1 at the end of this section shows the general site plan for the existing Winchester WTP.
Hydraulic Capacity Evaluation
General
The maximum raw water pumping rate with all raw water pumps operating is nominally 22 mgd; however, during a test on June 24, 2003, the total combined flow of all four raw water pumps was 20.9 mgd. The maximum instantaneous flow rate of finished water from the high service pump station is nominally 16 mgd with all finished water pumps operating; however, the maximum actually achieved is about 14 mgd.

[2 recommendation clause(s) withheld]

[p.108]
The plant currently operates continuously throughout each day on a “24/7” basis to keep the terminal reservoirs on Reservoir Hill full to meet demands in the City’s distribution system. The plant flow rate is typically adjusted on a daily basis, and occasionally more frequently when required, as water demands fluctuate. As discussed in Section 2, the plant flow rate has ranged from approximately 3.5 mgd during low demand periods to 11.6 mgd during a recent peak summer day.
Existing Hydraulic Profile
Figure 4-2 at the end of this section presents the hydraulic profile of the plant. The hydraulic profile was developed during the original design of the Winchester WTP for a maximum instantaneous flow of 18 mgd. Figure 4-1 has been updated, based on field tests conducted for this analysis, for a maximum flow of 22 mgd. The key hydraulic control features of the plant include:
River water levels and intake pumping capacity Hydraulic capacity of the 30-inch raw water pipeline to the flocculation/sedimentation basin Hydraulic capacity of the overflow weir at the outlet of the flocculation/sedimentation basin Hydraulic capacity of the 42-inch settled water pipeline delivering water to the filters Filter and pipe gallery hydraulics, including minimum water level inside the filters, for optimum performance and adequate available headloss for filter operations Filter underdrain and piping system capacity to the clearwell Hydraulic capacity of the overflow weir in the clearwell High service pumping capacity from the clearwell into the transmission system Finished water transmission pipeline capacity Backwash piping and pumping capacity Wastewater pump station and force main capacity Washwater and solids handling system capacity
Hydraulic capacity issues associated with each of these features are described in detail below.
Intake and Raw Water Pumping Capacity
The existing intake is equipped with 4 vertical turbine pumps, one with a capacity of 2,800 gpm (4.0 mgd) at 49 feet of total dynamic head (TDH) and three, each with a capacity of 4,200 gpm (6.0 mgd) at 49 feet of TDH. The smaller pump, Pump No. 1, has a 50 hp motor and the larger pumps, Pump Nos. 2, 3, and 4, have 75 hp motors.
All of the spaces provided for pumps are filled at the Winchester WTP intake. According to current planning and operating conventions within the water industry, firm pumping capacity is defined as the maximum flow achievable with one of the largest installed pumps out of service; therefore, the nominal firm capacity of the intake is approximately 16 mgd. Through such careful design, it may be possible to avoid raising the overflow weir on the existing basin. The ultimate hydraulic capacity of the two basins in parallel is limited primarily by the settled water pipeline and that ultimate capacity is 22 to 24 mgd.
Filters, Filter Effluent and Filter-to-Waste Piping
Section 2 provides basic information on the design and performance of the filters. Settled water flows through the filter influent channel and enters each filter via a 20-inch pipe with isolation valve. The normal filter operating level ranges from 463 to 464 feet as controlled by the filter effluent flow control system. This water level provides 5 to 6 feet of submergence over the top of the filter media. A filter effluent modulating valve is used to maintain this water level in each filter. As headloss increases, the valve opens further. Each filter consists of two bays. The water flows down through the media, the support gravel and the underdrain of each filter bay. The water then flows into the filter piping gallery through 16-inch pipes that individually drain each filter bay and is combined into an 18-inch filter effluent pipe that is common to the two bays within a filter. The filtered water flows through the 18-inch effluent pipe, a propeller flow meter, the filter effluent modulating butterfly valve and then into the unbaffled clearwell area underneath the filters. Each filter empties directly into the clearwell through its own 18-inch effluent pipe, thus each filter’s effluent enters the clearwell at a different location.
The normal maximum water level in the treated water storage area and clearwell is 449.0 feet, six-inches below the elevation of an overflow weir located beneath the high service pump station. The clearwell is normally operated between about 446.5 feet and 448 feet, which provides a total filter driving head of approximately 15 to 17.5 feet from filter water level to treated water storage level. The alarm signifying terminal filter headloss is currently set at 11.0 feet. Plans were made with the original design to add two more filters to expand capacity.
As discussed below, the current 3 mgd filter rating is a treatment capacity limitation rather than a hydraulic limitation. Hydraulically, the piping into and out of each basin can handle 4 mgd when the filter is filtering to the clearwell. With six filters, the total hydraulic capacity of the filters will be 24 mgd. Individual filter effluent flows into the clearwell are measured; however the requirements for straight-pipe both upstream and downstream of each filter effluent flow meter are not met, possibly reducing the accuracy of the meters. During a plant tour on September 14, 2006 the sum of the individual filter effluent meters was approximately 7 percent less than the flow determined by the more accurate magnetic flow meter measuring raw water flow.
The filter effluent piping arrangement currently prohibits the metering and modulating of filter-to-waste flows. Filter-to-waste flows can be estimated by calculating the difference between the raw water flow and the sum of the individual filter effluent flows. Based on this, it appears that the existing 8-inch filter-to-waste piping is too small to convey 3 mgd when filtering to waste. On a site visit to the plant on June 29, 2006, with filter No. 3 offline for
09-1015.401                                 Page 4-6                  WTP Preliminary Design Report
July 2009                                Capacity Review                           City of Roseburg

[p.113]
cleaning and a raw water flow of 9.1 mgd, the flow through filter No. 1 in filter-to-waste was estimated by calculating the difference between the raw water flow and the combined filter effluent flows through filters No. 2 and No. 4. The filter-to-waste flow was approximately 2 mgd while the flow through the other two filters was greater than 3.4 mgd.
It is desirable to modulate filter-to-waste flow to maintain relatively constant flow through all filters at all times. Rapid increases in flow through the media induce shear forces on the retained floc which can cause premature breakthrough. Inducing rapid flow changes in a conventional filter when the filter is operating near its treatment capacity is particularly problematic. When filter-to-waste piping is unable to pass the design filter flow, then the flow through all other filters on line increases while one filter is in filter-to-waste. This problem is more pronounced with fewer filters, when the filters are operating near their design flow and when the difference between the filter design flow and the filter-to-waste flow is high.
In addition to the hydraulic capacity limitations of the filter-to-waste piping, the current location of the filter effluent sample point prohibits measurement of turbidity during filter-to- waste. For all the above stated reasons, changes in the filter effluent and filter-to-waste piping are desirable.
Options for this work vary depending upon the extent to which the City desires to monitor and control filter-to-waste. It may be possible to achieve more accurate effluent flow measurement by simply installing a different meter while using the existing piping configuration. In addition, relocating the sample point would enable measurement of filter- to-waste turbidity; thus, the lowest cost option would be to change the type of effluent meter and the location of the sample point without reconfiguring the filter effluent piping. This option would not provide for measurement and control of filter-to-waste flow and it would not provide for the increased piping size needed to pass more than 2 mgd during filter-to- waste. To provide measurement and control of filter-to-waste flow, and to allow for filter-to- waste at the same rate as filtering to the clearwell, Although this is the more expensive alternative, it is the one that brings the greatest benefit.
Given that the existing filter-to-waste piping does not appear to convey more than 2 mgd, any plan to increase the WTP capacity beyond 18 mgd may require reconfiguring the piping since the difference between the existing filter-to-waste flow and the higher filter design flow would be even more pronounced.
Clearwell
The clearwell and treated water storage at the Winchester WTP are comprised of three interconnected areas described as follows:

There are two clearwell overflows, one located in the high service pump station and the other located below Filter No. 3. The high service pump station clearwell overflow weir is at elevation 449.5 feet with a weir length of approximately 9 feet. The high service pump station clearwell will overflow first until the water level exceeds 450.00 feet, then water will overflow both weirs. Combined, the two overflow weirs can accommodate an ultimate plant flow of 24 mgd.

Section 2 discussed the design features of the plant’s pretreatment system including rapid mix, flocculation and sedimentation. Settled solids from the basin are continuously removed by a chain-and-flight system. Settled water flows from the basin via the launders into a settled water channel located at the south end of the basin. The settled water then flows to the filters via a 42-inch pipeline.
The maximum water elevation in the basin is in the raw water influent channel. At 12 mgd, There is a triangular launder weir in the sedimentation basin with invert elevation of approximately 465.83 feet. The bottoms of the 12-inch deep launder troughs in the sedimentation basin are approximately elevation 464.63 feet. The freeboard from the top of maximum water surface to the top of walls is approximately 1.5 feet which is adequate.
The basin has an overflow weir to accommodate unplanned filter influent valve shutdowns or raw water flows into the basin that exceed the filter capacity. The overflow weir is located in the settled water collection channel at the south end of the basin above a disposal channel drained by a pipeline. The overflow weir elevation is at 465.0 feet, approximately 1.0 feet higher than the normal filter operating level. The weir is approximately 9 feet long with a capacity of approximately 12 mgd, assuming a 9-inch water depth over the weir. The drain pipe is 30-inches in diameter, has a capacity of approximately 10 mgd, and delivers this flow to a diversion manhole with a weir. Under normal conditions sedimentation basin overflows are directed to the wastewater pump station, but if the pump station cannot handle the flow the water flows over the weir inside the diversion manhole and then to the river. A second overflow weir will be constructed along with the second flocculation/sedimentation basin when the plant is expanded; thus, the overflow system is adequate for an ultimate maximum plant capacity of 24 mgd.
The settled water pipeline to the filters is a 42-inch diameter steel pipe. At 18 mgd the pipeline velocity will be 2.9 fps and at 24 mgd the pipeline velocity would be 3.9 fps. Although these velocities are not excessive, this pipe could be the largest contributor to headloss at high flows. During a flow test conducted on September 14, 2006, the head loss through the pipe was measured at 2.8-inches at a flow rate of 13.1 mgd. Under these conditions, the water surface in the settled water channel was approximately 6-inches below the basin overflow weir. Depending upon where the new settled water pipe connects to the existing settled water pipe, the head loss at 24 mgd would be several inches greater.

criteria.name: Study target - expand nominal 12 mgd to 18 mgd
criteria.source: p.111 - single existing basin is rated at 12 mgd and was designed to be expanded with a parallel basin for an ultimate nominal treatment capacity of 18 mgd
criteria.value: 12 mgd existing nominal, 18 mgd future nominal

criteria.name: Ultimate hydraulic basis for profile drawing
criteria.source: dwg p.136 Note 2. BASED ON AN ULTIMATE PLANT FLOW OF 22 MGD.

criteria.name: Ultimate hydraulic capacity of 2-basin pretreatment
criteria.source: p.111 - with approximately 24 mgd of hydraulic capacity; p.112 - ultimate hydraulic capacity of the two basins in parallel is limited primarily by the settled water pipeline and that ultimate capacity is 22 to 24 mgd
criteria.value: 22-24 mgd hydraulic, 18 mgd nominal treatment for 2 basins

criteria.name: Firm capacity definition
criteria.source: Engineering rules - Firm capacity = capacity with the largest unit of a station out of service

criteria.name: Raw-water pipeline max desirable velocity
criteria.source: p.110 - The maximum desirable velocity in a transmission main of this type is typically 6.0 fps.

criteria.name: Finished-water transmission velocity guide (same type main)
criteria.source: ASSUMPTION - p.110 states 6.0 fps for raw-water transmission main of this type; Table 4-3 p.117 shows 5.97 fps at 18 mgd with no exceedance stated, apply same 6.0 fps screen; to be confirmed by headloss/TDH analysis

criteria.name: Intake fish-protection approach velocity
criteria.source: p.109 - maximum approach velocity for protection of fish applies at these openings. With a maximum approach velocity of 0.4 fps and with the gates fully submerged
criteria.value: 0.4 fps at 4-ft square gated openings outside fish screens

criteria.name: Pretreatment freeboard adequacy
criteria.source: p.111 - The freeboard from the top of maximum water surface to the top of walls is approximately 1.5 feet which is adequate.

criteria.name: Basin overflow weir datum
criteria.source: p.111 - The overflow weir elevation is at 465.0 feet, approximately 1.0 feet higher than the normal filter operating level.
criteria.value: 465.0 ft, ~1.0 ft above normal filter level

criteria.name: Normal filter operating level
criteria.source: p.112 - The normal filter operating level ranges from 463 to 464 feet

criteria.name: Filter-to-waste operation objective
criteria.source: p.113 - It is desirable to modulate filter-to-waste flow to maintain relatively constant flow through all filters at all times.
criteria.value: constant flow through all filters, avoid rapid increases/shear/breakthrough

criteria.name: Clearwell operating levels
criteria.source: dwg p.136 - NORMAL HIGH WS IN CLEARWELL 449.0 NORMAL OPERATING LEVEL 446.5 TO 448.0 DEPENDING UPON HYDRAULIC EFFICIENCY AFTER EXPANSION AND UPON CHLORINE RESIDUAL MAINTAINED.

criteria.name: Clearwell storage datum at max depth
criteria.source: p.114 - maximum storage volume ... at 10.5 foot water depth ... total maximum ... 627,000 gallons represents approximately 75 minutes (1.26 hours) of storage at the current maximum
criteria.value: 627,000 gal at 10.5 ft = 75 min at current max (~12 mgd)

criteria.name: Backwash redundancy
criteria.source: p.118-p.119 - Only one pump is required for backwashing each of the filter bays. The second pump serves as a spare/backup

criteria.name: Wastewater pump station firm basis
criteria.source: p.119 - approximate firm capacity of this station is 3,000 gpm with one of the pumps out of service.

criteria.name: Surge protection design criteria
criteria.source: p.117 - Surge protection is provided for pumping rates up to 9,700 gpm (14.0 mgd) The maximum upsurge ... is controlled to 150 psi. The minimum allowable downsurge at the high service pump station is controlled to an HGL of 630 feet (approximately 175 feet of head or 75 psi assuming plant ground elevation of 455 feet.)
criteria.value: 14.0 mgd, 150 psi max upsurge, HGL 630 ft min downsurge at HSPS

criteria.name: Hydraulic vs treatment capacity distinction
criteria.source: p.107 - The hydraulic capacity is related to the piping, pumping, volume and flow control systems ... The treatment capacity is related to the ability of each treatment unit process to meet regulatory requirements

data_register.item: River intake - gated openings to river
data_register.quote: The intake structure has four gated openings to the North Umpqua River, each 4 feet square.
data_register.value: 4 openings, each 4x4 ft

data_register.quote: There are two traveling screens which screen the raw water before it enters the pump bay. These screens will pass up to 18 mgd or more of raw water.
data_register.value: up to 18 mgd or more (2 screens)

data_register.item: River intake - openings screens to pump bay
data_register.quote: There are two 5 feet square gated openings between the traveling screens and the pump bay. These openings are of adequate size to supply the intake pumps with up to 24 mgd or more
data_register.value: 2 openings, each 5x5 ft, adequate to 24 mgd or more

data_register.quote: These openings are of adequate size to supply the intake pumps with up to 24 mgd or more of raw water.
data_register.value: 4x4-ft openings adequate to 24 mgd or more (hydraulically, before fish-velocity limit)

data_register.quote: The maximum velocity in the intake outside the traveling screens occurs at the 4 feet square gated openings. As discussed in Section 3, because these openings are located outside the fish screens, the maximum approach velocity for protection of fish applies at these openings. With a maximum approach velocity of 0.4 fps and with the gates fully submerged
data_register.value: 0.4 fps max approach at 4-ft openings, gates fully submerged

data_register.item: Raw water pump station - 2006 demonstrated capacity 3 pumps
data_register.quote: On September 14, 2006 with Pump Nos. 1, 2 and 4 operating, the intake provided only 14 mgd.
data_register.value: 14 mgd with Pump Nos. 1,2,4 operating

data_register.item: Raw water pump station - 2002 firm capacity test
data_register.quote: Testing of the station in 2002 determined that the firm capacity of the station at that time was approximately 15.0 mgd.
data_register.value: approx 15.0 mgd firm (2002)

data_register.quote: The 2002 test results appear to indicate that Pump No. 3 is pumping substantially below its rated capacity; however, Pump No. 3 was not operating during the test on September 14, 2006 and the capacity was even lower.
data_register.value: Pump No.3 substantially below rated (2002); not operating 2006 yet capacity lower

data_register.quote: The City recently installed a VFD on Pump No. 2.
data_register.value: VFD on Pump No.2 installed; plus VFDs on one raw and one finished pump being installed per p.115

data_register.item: Raw water pipeline - diameter, material, wall
data_register.quote: The raw water pumps discharge into an underground 30-inch diameter steel raw water pipeline ... The steel pipe has a 1/4-inch wall thickness.
data_register.value: 30-in steel, 1/4-in wall

data_register.quote: A 30-inch magnetic flow meter was installed on this pipeline in a below-grade vault in 2002
data_register.value: 30-in mag meter (2002)

data_register.item: Rapid mix basins - two parallel, one operated
data_register.quote: There are two rapid mix basins in parallel, but currently only one rapid mixer is operated at any given time.
data_register.value: 2 basins parallel, 1 operated currently

data_register.quote: Under those conditions, both rapid mix basins will be operated in parallel at the higher flows.
data_register.value: both basins in parallel at higher (18 mgd) flows

data_register.quote: The single existing basin is rated at 12 mgd
data_register.value: 12 mgd single basin

data_register.quote: was designed to be expanded with a parallel basin for an ultimate nominal treatment capacity of 18 mgd, but with approximately 24 mgd of hydraulic capacity.
data_register.value: 18 mgd nominal, ~24 mgd hydraulic (2 basins)

data_register.quote: this basin has been able to provide excellent pretreatment prior to filtration at sustained flows up to 11.5 mgd during the warm weather, low turbidity raw water conditions.
data_register.value: up to 11.5 mgd sustained demonstrated

data_register.quote: Normal plant flows during high turbidity, colder water conditions have ranged from 3.5 to 5.0 mgd.

data_register.item: Sed basin launder weir and trough elevations
data_register.quote: There is a triangular launder weir in the sedimentation basin with invert elevation of approximately 465.83 feet. The bottoms of the 12-inch deep launder troughs in the sedimentation basin are approximately elevation 464.63 feet.
data_register.value: launder weir invert ~465.83; trough bottoms ~464.63 (12-in deep troughs)

data_register.quote: The freeboard from the top of maximum water surface to the top of walls is approximately 1.5 feet which is adequate.
data_register.value: ~1.5 ft adequate

data_register.item: Sed basin overflow weir elevation and relation to filters
data_register.quote: The overflow weir elevation is at 465.0 feet, approximately 1.0 feet higher than the normal filter operating level.
data_register.value: 465.0 ft, ~1.0 ft above normal filter level

data_register.item: Sed basin overflow weir length and capacity
data_register.quote: The weir is approximately 9 feet long with a capacity of approximately 12 mgd, assuming a 9-inch water depth over the weir.
data_register.value: ~9 ft long, ~12 mgd at 9-in depth

data_register.item: Sed basin overflow drain pipe capacity and routing
data_register.quote: The drain pipe is 30-inches in diameter, has a capacity of approximately 10 mgd, and delivers this flow to a diversion manhole with a weir. Under normal conditions sedimentation basin overflows are directed to the wastewater pump station, but if the pump station cannot handle the flow the water flows over the weir inside the diversion manhole and then to the river.
data_register.value: 30-in drain ~10 mgd to diversion MH with weir; normal to WWPS, excess to river

data_register.quote: A second overflow weir will be constructed along with the second flocculation/sedimentation basin when the plant is expanded; thus, the overflow system is adequate for an ultimate maximum plant capacity of 24 mgd.
data_register.value: 2 weirs adequate to 24 mgd ultimate max

data_register.item: Settled water pipeline to filters - diameter and velocities
data_register.quote: The settled water pipeline to the filters is a 42-inch diameter steel pipe. At 18 mgd the pipeline velocity will be 2.9 fps and at 24 mgd the pipeline velocity would be 3.9 fps.

definitions.definition: Nominal capacity is treatment-rated flow meeting regulatory/loading criteria; hydraulic capacity is ability to pass flow through piping/pumping/volumes; firm capacity is with largest unit out of service.

submit.question: Can the Winchester WTP be expanded from its current 12 mgd to 18 mgd? For each unit along the flow path, determine whether it limits 18 mgd, the flow at which it becomes limiting, and the least-cost modification that makes 18 mgd work.

rfi.issue: Raw-water pump rated Q/TDH, pump count, and firm vs nominal unknown; 2002 firm 15.0 mgd conflicts with 2006 14 mgd with 3 pumps and Pump 3 deficiency cause unknown; VFD scope incomplete.
rfi.reason: Cannot compute station TDH at 18 mgd with higher raw-pipeline HL (Table 4-1) without pump curves, ages, and N-1 basis
rfi.resolution: ASSUMPTION with reason: For 18-mgd screening assume firm capacity is governed by demonstrated ~14-15 mgd (p.109) and station LIMITS 18 mgd until proven otherwise, because demonstrated test is more conservative than any unstated nameplate; assume 4 pumps with largest out (N-1) as firm basis per rules. Reason: protects against over-crediting untested nameplates given Pump 3 deficiency and lower 2006 result.

rfi.issue: High-service pump count, rated Q/TDH, firm capacity, and system HGL to Reservoir Hill (710 ft) not in available pages; VFD scope and transmission completion status unclear.
rfi.reason: Cannot determine flow at which HSPS/transmission binds 18 mgd without pump curves and system headloss to elev 710
rfi.resolution: ASSUMPTION with reason: Assume HSPS + transmission LIMITS 18 mgd pending data, because surge design only to 14.0 mgd (p.117) and report notes higher head may be needed >18 mgd and phased 30-in parallels may be incomplete (p.118); assume least-cost is staged pump + pipeline phasing, not site short main. Reason: avoids assuming unbuilt transmission capacity.

rfi.issue: Filter number, area, media, design loading rate (gpm/sf), N-1 firm filtration rate, backwash duration, and effluent/FTW piping ratings not in available pages; only 4-filter implication (clearwell zone 1 under four filters p.114) and 20-in influents/463-464 ft level given.
rfi.item: Filters, filter effluent and filter-to-waste piping
rfi.reason: Cannot compute loading at 12 vs 18 mgd or with one filter out/wasting without area and rating
rfi.resolution: ASSUMPTION with reason: Assume 4 filter bays (per under the four filters p.114) and assume existing filters are treatment-rated near 12 mgd total so 18 mgd REQUIRES additional filter area or higher-rate media proof, because single-basin pretreatment rated 12 mgd (p.111) implies matched filter nominal. Reason: prevents assuming higher-rate filtration without regulatory proof; field test must establish loading/breakthrough.

rfi.issue: Rapid-mix basin volume, detention, mixer G/power, and headloss at 18 mgd (both basins parallel) missing; drawing levels 467.5/466.0/454.0 single-read.
rfi.reason: Cannot verify detention/G or water-surface vs freeboard at 18 mgd
rfi.resolution: ASSUMPTION with reason: Assume rapid mix does NOT limit 18 mgd hydraulically if both basins operated parallel as intended (p.110), but treatment (G/detention) must be verified by test. Reason: parallel operation halves velocity per basin; least-cost is operate both, no new basin assumed until test fails.

rfi.issue: Floc/sed detention, SOR, weir loading at 12 vs 9 mgd per basin (18 mgd/2) missing; max influent-channel WS at 12 mgd sentence truncated; launder invert 465.83 vs trough bottom 464.63 appears inverted (invert above bottom) - conflict; drawing MAX WS 465.95 vs OF 465.00 single-read.
rfi.reason: Cannot find limiting flow for SOR/weir/freeboard without geometry and criteria
rfi.resolution: ASSUMPTION with reason: Assume second parallel basin as planned (p.110-p.111) makes 18 mgd (9 mgd/basin) TREATMENT-adequate for study, but hydraulic limit 22-24 mgd set by settled-water pipe (p.112) governs; flag launder-elev conflict as drafting/definition error to confirm in field, do not use 465.83 for head calc until confirmed. Reason: uses report-stated 18 mgd nominal / 24 mgd hydraulic intent while quarantining suspect elev.

rfi.issue: Settled-water 42-in pipeline length, C-factor, connection point for second basin, and HL at 18 mgd not given beyond 2.8-in at 13.1 mgd and 6-in below weir; ultimate 22-24 mgd stated but calculation basis missing.
rfi.reason: Cannot calibrate run_profile/profile_capacity without length/C and tie-in
rfi.resolution: ASSUMPTION with reason: Assume single 42-in calibration point (2.8-in at 13.1 mgd p.111) is representative and assume HL scales with flow per Table-type hydraulics to be verified, with limit 22-24 mgd per p.112 accepted as report-given. Reason: only field-measured HL available; must re-measure at higher flow before design.

rfi.issue: Intake approach-velocity flow limit redacted ([withheld] To achieve greater intake capacity p.109); river levels vs opening submergence at low water (dwg 432/420/415.5/408.0 single-read) and trash-rack/screen headloss missing.
rfi.reason: Cannot compute Q at 0.4 fps without submerged opening area at design low water
rfi.resolution: ASSUMPTION with reason: Assume intake fish-velocity LIMITS below 18 mgd until field proves submergence/area, because 0.4 fps on 4x 4-ft openings is highly restrictive at low river stage and screens only pass up to 18 mgd or more (p.109, marginal wording). Reason: fish criterion is regulatory and wording or more indicates no margin; least-cost likely opening/screen expansion per Sec 6 options.

rfi.issue: Raw and finished pipeline headloss basis (length, Hazen-Williams C, fittings, meter loss) not given for Table 4-1/4-3; cannot independently verify 0.25 ft/100ft at 18 mgd or station TDH increase.
rfi.reason: Need length/C to model pumped legs in run_hydraulics and gravity legs in run_profile
rfi.resolution: ASSUMPTION with reason: For screening accept Table 4-1/4-3 velocities/HL as report-given design values (p.110/p.117) without recomputing, to be calibrated by field differential-pressure test. Reason: avoids silent invention of C/length; uses document units/values directly.

rfi.issue: Clearwell CT/baffling factor, required detention at 18 mgd, inlet/outlet hydraulics, and operating depth vs 10.5 ft max missing; 75 min at current max implies ~50 min at 18 mgd but disinfectant credit unknown.
rfi.reason: Cannot determine if 627k gal with unbaffled/baffled zones meets regulation at 18 mgd
rfi.resolution: ASSUMPTION with reason: Assume clearwell VOLUME is adequate for flow (75 min at ~12 mgd => ~50 min at 18 mgd) but CT LIMITS unless baffling/chlorine proves otherwise, because two zones are unbaffled (p.114). Reason: volume alone does not equal CT; conservative for health-based criterion.

rfi.issue: Surge adequacy 14.0 to 18 mgd missing; second tank impractical (space p.117) but alternative mitigation (VFD ramp, controls, relief, tank retune) not sized.
rfi.reason: Cannot state limiting flow or least-cost fix without transient reanalysis to 150 psi / HGL 630 ft criteria
rfi.resolution: ASSUMPTION with reason: Assume existing single 1,900 cu ft tank LIMITS at 14.0 mgd rating (p.117) and 18 mgd REQUIRES reanalysis + controls/relief upgrade, not second tank, because report states second tank likely not practical due to space. Reason: respects stated space constraint and rated limit.

rfi.issue: Wastewater pump station inflow at 18 mgd (backwash volume/frequency + sed sludge + overflows) vs 3,000 gpm firm and 30-in drain 10 mgd vs 9-ft weir 12 mgd mismatch; basin decant/drying capacity at 18 mgd missing.
rfi.reason: Cannot balance backwash/sludge water at higher filter and basin throughput without production rates
rfi.resolution: ASSUMPTION with reason: Assume WWPS firm 3,000 gpm (p.119) is ADEQUATE for normal 18-mgd backwash if sequencing unchanged (one filter at a time, 3,250 gpm backwash pump p.119, short duration), but overflow drain (10 mgd pipe vs 12 mgd weir) LIMITS single-basin overflow until second weir built with second basin (p.111). Reason: distinguishes short-duration backwash pumping from continuous overflow drainage; second weir is already planned least-cost.

rfi.issue: All drawing water-surface/structure elevations except 453.0 high water are single-read and need confirmation; especially sed MAX WS 465.95, WS 464.83, filter 464.0, clearwell 449.0/446.5-448.0, WWPS 440.3, diversion MH, settling basins MAX WS 458.0, reservoir 710.0.
rfi.reason: Cannot calibrate profile against drawing_ws_ft at drawing design flow 22 mgd without confirmed datums; residuals would be spurious
rfi.resolution: ASSUMPTION with reason: For Step 1 assume text elevations govern over drawing where conflict (e.g., OF 465.0 p.111, filter 463-464 p.112, clearwell 627k gal basis), and treat all dwg values except 453.0 as UNCONFIRMED single-read to be surveyed. Reason: text has explicit context and freeboard statements; drawing is schematic with finish-grade approximation (Note 1).

rfi.issue: Chemical feed (ACH, NaOCl, pH, carbon slurry, filter-aid polymer) capacities at 18 mgd, plus filter-aid/NaOCl points shown on dwg, not in available pages.
rfi.reason: Pretreatment/filter expansion to 18 mgd may be chemical-limited
rfi.resolution: ASSUMPTION with reason: Assume chemical systems REQUIRE upsizing review but do NOT govern 18-mgd feasibility screening, to be inventoried on site. Reason: no data to find limiting flow; cannot silently assume adequate.

standards.name: Overflow/freeboard: OF 465.0 (~1 ft above filter level), 1.5 ft freeboard adequate, 9-ft weir ~12 mgd at 9-in depth, 30-in drain ~10 mgd (p.111)
standards.use: pretreatment hydraulic limits and N-1 overflow routing

standards.name: Surge: 14.0 mgd, 150 psi upsurge, HGL 630 ft downsurge at HSPS (p.117)

test_plan.acceptance: Pump Q within 5% of curve at measured TDH; firm (N-1) >=18 mgd required to clear RFI; if <18 mgd intake/pumps limit confirmed
test_plan.measurements: River level, pump suction/discharge pressure, flow by 30-in mag meter + clamp-on check, amps/volts, VFD Hz, valve positions, pump combo (including N-1 combos and Pump 3 alone)
test_plan.procedure: Step-test each pump alone then combos 1-2-4, 1-2-3, etc. at normal and low river stage; record TDH vs Q; compare 2002 15.0 mgd and 2006 14 mgd baselines; inspect Pump 3 wear/clearance
test_plan.purpose: Establish rated vs field firm capacity and TDH at 18 mgd with Table 4-1 HL
test_plan.test: T-RWPS: raw-water pump station TDH-Q test

test_plan.acceptance: Approach velocity <=0.4 fps at 18 mgd demand with gates fully submerged; else intake limits and Sec 6 expansion required
test_plan.measurements: River stage, gate openings/submergence, velocity traverse at each 4x4-ft opening and at screens, trash-rack differential, flow (plant mag meter)
test_plan.procedure: ADCP/velocity meter traverse across 4 openings at 3 plant flows up to max available; compute Q/area vs 0.4 fps; survey opening inverts and low-water submergence
test_plan.purpose: Find Q at 0.4 fps binding limit

test_plan.acceptance: HL per 100 ft within 15% of Table 4-1/4-3 at test flow; calibrated C/length then used for 18-mgd TDH; velocity >6.0 fps flags modification
test_plan.measurements: Differential pressure/flow over known length for 30-in raw and 30-in finished site main at 3 flows; record temperature, valve/meter losses
test_plan.procedure: Pressure gauges upstream/downstream of test reach + mag meter flow; 30-min steady at each flow; compute ft/100ft vs Table values
test_plan.purpose: Calibrate run_hydraulics pumped legs and verify 5.9/5.97 fps at 18 mgd
test_plan.test: T-PIPE: raw + finished site-main HL test

test_plan.acceptance: Levels stable below OF 465.0 with >=1.0 ft margin to filter level and >=1.5 ft freeboard at 18 mgd (2 basins); HL vs 2.8-in at 13.1 mgd baseline consistent
test_plan.closes_rfi: Flocculation/sedimentation performance and levels; Settled water pipeline calibration
test_plan.measurements: Influent-channel WS, settled-channel WS, launder/trough WS, filter level, settled 42-in flow and differential HL, overflow weir/drain flow if any
test_plan.procedure: Staged flow test (if available to ~13-14 mgd single basin + model to 9 mgd/basin two-basin); survey weir/trough inverts (resolve 465.83 vs 464.63 conflict) and wall tops; dye/tracer for short-circuiting
test_plan.purpose: Calibrate run_profile gravity leg and find Q where OF/freeboard binds; confirm 22-24 mgd pipe limit

test_plan.acceptance: Loading <= approved gpm/sf with one filter out and one in FTW (~2 mgd waste per p.113); turbidity/breakthrough criteria met; else filters limit 18 mgd
test_plan.closes_rfi: Filters, filter effluent and filter-to-waste piping
test_plan.measurements: Per-filter flow, influent channel level (463-464 ft datum), effluent turbidity/particle counts, headloss, backwash rate/duration, FTW flow/modulation, valve timing
test_plan.procedure: Load test at max available flow with one filter in FTW; step flows; record >3.4 mgd/filter behavior noted p.113; survey media depth/type and measure area
test_plan.purpose: Determine firm filtration capacity and Q-limit to 18 mgd; size added area or high-rate media need
test_plan.test: T-FLT: filter loading + FTW modulation test

test_plan.acceptance: CT ratio >=1.0 at 18 mgd through baffled volume at operating depth 446.5-448.0 ft with maintained chlorine residual; else clearwell/CT limits
test_plan.measurements: Clearwell levels, in/out flows, chlorine residual in/out, temperature/pH, tracer or level-volume curve to verify 170k/324k/133k gal at 10.5 ft
test_plan.procedure: Volume survey + flow-through test; compute detention at 12 vs 18 mgd (75 min baseline p.114); coordinate with State for baffling factor and required CT

units_on_path: RIVER INTAKE - gated river openings, trash rack, traveling screens, pump-bay openings, raw water pumps
RAW WATER PIPELINE - 30-in steel + 30-in mag meter to floc/sed basin NE corner
RAPID MIX - 2 basins parallel (1 operated now, 2 at high flows)

FLOCCULATION / SEDIMENTATION BASIN - existing 12-mgd basin + future 2nd parallel (18 mgd nominal, 24 mgd hydraulic), chain-flight, launders, settled channel, 9-ft overflow weir + 30-in drain to diversion MH
SETTLED WATER PIPELINE - 42-in steel to filters
FILTERS - influent channel, 20-in influent per filter, filter bays (4 implied), effluent + filter-to-waste piping
CLEARWELL - zone 1 under filters unbaffled, zone 2 baffled under chemical/blower rooms, zone 3 unbaffled under HS room

Avoid suction lift; if unavoidable keep it preferably under 15 ft and provide priming.
Dedicated standby power so water can be treated and/or pumped to meet average day demand during outages.
Distribution system holds at least 20 psi at ground level at all points under all flow conditions.
Normal working pressure should be about 60-80 psi and not less than 35 psi.
Where static pressure exceeds 100 psi, pressure reducing devices are required.
Minimum water main diameter 6 in where fire protection/hydrants are served; 3 in where no fire protection.
Air relief valves required at high points of water mains where air can accumulate.
Intake influent velocity 0.5 ft/s or less where frazil ice may form.
Rapid mix: instantaneous, not longer than 30 s, with velocity gradient G of at least 750 /s.
Flocculation detention time should be at least 30 minutes.
Flow-through velocity in flocculation basins 0.5 to 1.5 ft/min.
Conventional sedimentation provides at least 4 h settling time (reductions only with demonstration or SOR <= 0.5 gpm/sf).
Horizontal velocity through sedimentation basin should not exceed 0.5 ft/min.
Outlet weir/launder or submerged orifice collector loading not more than 20,000 gpd per ft.
Typical rapid-rate gravity filtration rates 2 to 4 gpm/sf; any rate must be justified to the reviewing authority (advisory range, not a hard cap).
At least two filters; with more than two, design capacity met with the largest filter out of service.
Filter box at least 8.5 ft deep with at least 3 ft of water over the media.
Backwash rate at least 15 gpm/sf (20 gpm/sf or 50% bed expansion recommended).
Clearwell has at least two compartments (50% isolatable); sized for disinfectant contact time.
Hydropneumatic tank gross volume (gal) at least 10 x largest pump capacity (gpm), unless VFDs etc. meet max demand.
Multiple pumps; with any unit out of service the remaining units handle design peak hourly flow; with two units both equal size.
Wet well effective volume based on design average flow and fill time not exceeding 30 min; minimum cycle time per pump maker's duty cycle.
Suction-lift stations: dynamic suction lift at pump-off plus NPSHr at design conditions not more than 22 ft.
Emergency pumping capability (unless storage prevents overflow), able to start and maintain total rated running capacity; portable pump connection always provided.
Force main cleansing velocity at design pumping rate at least 2 ft/s.
Force main velocity at most 8 ft/s recommended (head loss, valve protection).
Raw wastewater force main diameter not less than 4 in.
Air relief valves at force main high points; evaluate vacuum relief.
Hazen-Williams design C = 100 for unlined iron/steel; not more than 120 for PVC, PE, lined DI.
Primary settling surface overflow rate not over 1,000 gpd/sf at design average flow (1,500-2,000 at peak hourly; 700/1,200 if receiving WAS).

Minimum side water depth 10 ft primary, 12 ft secondary after activated sludge.

[p.110]
Raw Water Pipeline Capacity to the Flocculation/Sedimentation Basin
The raw water pumps discharge into an underground 30-inch diameter steel raw water pipeline which delivers raw water to the flocculation/sedimentation basin, entering on the northeast corner of the structure. The steel pipe has a ¼-inch wall thickness. A 30-inch magnetic flow meter was installed on this pipeline in a below-grade vault in 2002, replacing a meter previously located at the inlet of the raw water pipeline into the rapid mix basin. The velocity, velocity head and head loss for the existing raw water pipeline at various flows are presented in Table 4-1.
TABLE 4-1 30-INCH RAW WATER PIPELINE VELOCITIES AND HEADLOSS
Plant Flow (mgd)           Velocity              V2/2g            Headloss
(fps)                 (ft)            (ft/100 ft)
8                             2.6                 0.116               0.05
12                            3.9                  0.24               0.11
18                            5.9                  0.54               0.25
20                            6.5                  0.66               0.32
24                            7.8                  0.90               0.44
As shown in the table, velocities through the 30-inch raw water pipeline exceed 6.0 fps at flows slightly over 18 mgd. The maximum desirable velocity in a transmission main of this type is typically 6.0 fps. even at the higher velocities that will exist above 18 mgd. The headloss associated with higher flow through the existing pipeline will ultimately raise the system total dynamic head (TDH), thus reducing the capacity of the raw water pump station. To account for this, replacing pumps with a higher pumping head may be necessary to compensate for this increased headloss. If the plant is expanded beyond 18 mgd, there will be an opportunity to adjust the design head as necessary at that time.
Rapid Mix and Flocculation/Sedimentation Basin
Raw water flows first into a rapid mix basin and then into the flocculation/sedimentation basin. There are two rapid mix basins in parallel, but currently only one rapid mixer is operated at any given time. The basin design provides for the addition of a second, parallel flocculation and sedimentation basin to increase the plant capacity to a nominal 18 mgd. Under those conditions, both rapid mix basins will be operated in parallel at the higher flows.

[p.111]
Section 2 discussed the design features of the plant’s pretreatment system including rapid mix, flocculation and sedimentation. The single existing basin is rated at 12 mgd and was designed to be expanded with a parallel basin for an ultimate nominal treatment capacity of 18 mgd, but with approximately 24 mgd of hydraulic capacity. As previously discussed, this basin has been able to provide excellent pretreatment prior to filtration at sustained flows up to 11.5 mgd during the warm weather, low turbidity raw water conditions. Normal plant flows during high turbidity, colder water conditions have ranged from 3.5 to 5.0 mgd.
Settled solids from the basin are continuously removed by a chain-and-flight system. Settled water flows from the basin via the launders into a settled water channel located at the south end of the basin. The settled water then flows to the filters via a 42-inch pipeline.
The maximum water elevation in the basin is in the raw water influent channel. At 12 mgd, There is a triangular launder weir in the sedimentation basin with invert elevation of approximately 465.83 feet. The bottoms of the 12-inch deep launder troughs in the sedimentation basin are approximately elevation 464.63 feet. The freeboard from the top of maximum water surface to the top of walls is approximately 1.5 feet which is adequate.
The basin has an overflow weir to accommodate unplanned filter influent valve shutdowns or raw water flows into the basin that exceed the filter capacity. The overflow weir is located in the settled water collection channel at the south end of the basin above a disposal channel drained by a pipeline. The overflow weir elevation is at 465.0 feet, approximately 1.0 feet higher than the normal filter operating level. The weir is approximately 9 feet long with a capacity of approximately 12 mgd, assuming a 9-inch water depth over the weir. The drain pipe is 30-inches in diameter, has a capacity of approximately 10 mgd, and delivers this flow to a diversion manhole with a weir. Under normal conditions sedimentation basin overflows are directed to the wastewater pump station, but if the pump station cannot handle the flow the water flows over the weir inside the diversion manhole and then to the river. A second overflow weir will be constructed along with the second flocculation/sedimentation basin when the plant is expanded; thus, the overflow system is adequate for an ultimate maximum plant capacity of 24 mgd.
The settled water pipeline to the filters is a 42-inch diameter steel pipe. At 18 mgd the pipeline velocity will be 2.9 fps and at 24 mgd the pipeline velocity would be 3.9 fps. Although these velocities are not excessive, this pipe could be the largest contributor to headloss at high flows. During a flow test conducted on September 14, 2006, the head loss through the pipe was measured at 2.8-inches at a flow rate of 13.1 mgd. Under these conditions, the water surface in the settled water channel was approximately 6-inches below the basin overflow weir. Depending upon where the new settled water pipe connects to the existing settled water pipe, the head loss at 24 mgd would be several inches greater.

Through such careful design, it may be possible to avoid raising the overflow weir on the existing basin. The ultimate hydraulic capacity of the two basins in parallel is limited primarily by the settled water pipeline and that ultimate capacity is 22 to 24 mgd.
Filters, Filter Effluent and Filter-to-Waste Piping
Section 2 provides basic information on the design and performance of the filters. Settled water flows through the filter influent channel and enters each filter via a 20-inch pipe with isolation valve. The normal filter operating level ranges from 463 to 464 feet as controlled by the filter effluent flow control system. This water level provides 5 to 6 feet of submergence over the top of the filter media. A filter effluent modulating valve is used to maintain this water level in each filter. As headloss increases, the valve opens further. Each filter consists of two bays. The water flows down through the media, the support gravel and the underdrain of each filter bay. The water then flows into the filter piping gallery through 16-inch pipes that individually drain each filter bay and is combined into an 18-inch filter effluent pipe that is common to the two bays within a filter. The filtered water flows through the 18-inch effluent pipe, a propeller flow meter, the filter effluent modulating butterfly valve and then into the unbaffled clearwell area underneath the filters. Each filter empties directly into the clearwell through its own 18-inch effluent pipe, thus each filter’s effluent enters the clearwell at a different location.
The normal maximum water level in the treated water storage area and clearwell is 449.0 feet, six-inches below the elevation of an overflow weir located beneath the high service pump station. The clearwell is normally operated between about 446.5 feet and 448 feet, which provides a total filter driving head of approximately 15 to 17.5 feet from filter water level to treated water storage level. The alarm signifying terminal filter headloss is currently set at 11.0 feet. Plans were made with the original design to add two more filters to expand capacity.
As discussed below, the current 3 mgd filter rating is a treatment capacity limitation rather than a hydraulic limitation. Hydraulically, the piping into and out of each basin can handle 4 mgd when the filter is filtering to the clearwell. With six filters, the total hydraulic capacity of the filters will be 24 mgd. Individual filter effluent flows into the clearwell are measured; however the requirements for straight-pipe both upstream and downstream of each filter effluent flow meter are not met, possibly reducing the accuracy of the meters. During a plant tour on September 14, 2006 the sum of the individual filter effluent meters was approximately 7 percent less than the flow determined by the more accurate magnetic flow meter measuring raw water flow.
The filter effluent piping arrangement currently prohibits the metering and modulating of filter-to-waste flows. Filter-to-waste flows can be estimated by calculating the difference between the raw water flow and the sum of the individual filter effluent flows. Based on this, it appears that the existing 8-inch filter-to-waste piping is too small to convey 3 mgd when filtering to waste. On a site visit to the plant on June 29, 2006, with filter No. 3 offline for
